juju · Phase 2 · Web SDK

Why the web SDK looks like this

The server can receive errors, but nothing sends them yet. An SDK is the code a developer adds to their app so that crashes are caught and sent to juju automatically. Each part of Phase 2 solves one piece of that.

[phase 2] NEXT pkg=@juju/core,@juju/web done_when="an error thrown offline arrives exactly once after reconnecting"
Structure

Two packages: what to send, and how to catch it

Half of an SDK doesn't depend on where it runs: building events, queueing, sending, retrying. The other half is platform-specific: how you find out an error happened. Splitting them means React Native (Phase 3) reuses the first half instead of rewriting it, and a retry bug fixed once is fixed in both.

@juju/core

Plain JavaScript, no browser APIs.

  • event builder and stack trace parser
  • queue, batching, retry with backoff
  • breadcrumb ring buffer

@juju/web

Browser-only hooks on top of core.

  • window.onerror, unhandledrejection
  • sendBeacon when the page is hidden
  • console, fetch, click and route breadcrumbs

It's the same idea as the Go server's small Queue interface: separate what happens from how it happens.

@juju/core

Getting events to the server reliably

Event builder

Turns a JavaScript Error into exactly the v1 envelope the server validates. It parses the browser's stack trace text into the frames that fingerprinting relies on:

// what the browser gives you (Chrome's format; Firefox's differs)
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'price')
    at lineTotal (https://shop.example.com/assets/index.4b8c2d1e.js:1:48213)

// what the server receives
{ "function": "lineTotal", "filename": "https://shop.example.com/assets/index.4b8c2d1e.js",
  "lineno": 1, "colno": 48213, "in_app": true }
Connects to the serverThe builder creates event_id when the error happens, not when it's sent. Every retry carries the same ID, which is what lets the server's ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING recognize a retry. A new ID per send attempt would turn every retry into a duplicate.

In-memory queue

Errors go into a list first, never straight onto the network.

WhySending must never block or break the host app. If juju's server is down, the customer's app keeps working as if nothing happened.

Batching

Collect events for about 5 seconds, or until there are 20, then send them in one envelope.

WhyA render loop that throws 60 times a second would otherwise make 60 requests a second, using up the user's network and battery and hammering your server.
Connects to the serverThis is why the server accepts up to 100 events per envelope, and why it keeps the good events when one in a batch is bad.

Retry with backoff

When a send fails, wait, retry, and wait longer each time. A little randomness (jitter) is added to each wait.

send
+1s
+2s
+4s
+8s
+16s ✓
0s
8s
16s
24s
32s
○ failed attempt● deliveredExample timing, shown without jitter
WhyPhones lose signal constantly, so a failed send is normal. Backoff stops thousands of apps from hammering the server the moment it recovers, which would turn a short outage into a second one. Jitter stops them all retrying at the same second.

The status code contract

The SDK decides what to do from the server's reply. The server and SDK are two halves of one design, and this table is where they meet.

Server saysMeaningSDK does
202Stored or queueddelete
400 401 413 415Broken request; a retry can never succeeddelete and log a warning
429Server busykeep and wait at least Retry-After
5xx · network errorTemporary failurekeep and retry with backoff
@juju/web

Catching errors in the browser

window.onerror

Fires for any error nobody caught, like calling undefined() in a click handler. This one hook catches most crashes without the developer changing their code.

unhandledrejection

Modern code is full of async/await and fetch().then(…). When a Promise fails and nobody wrote .catch(), onerror does not fire. The browser raises this separate event instead.

WhyWithout it you'd miss every failed API call inside an async function, often the most common error in a web app.

Both hooks must call any handler that was already installed, and must never swallow the error. The developer's own error handling, or another tool they use, has to keep working. The /verify skill checks for this.

sendBeacon when the page is hidden

A user hits an error and closes the tab at once. A normal fetch gets cancelled as the page goes away, and the queued events die with it. navigator.sendBeacon() hands the data to the browser, which delivers it after the page is gone.

Why visibilitychange, not unloadMobile browsers often never fire unload (for example when you switch apps), but they do fire visibilitychange when the page becomes hidden.
Small server change this phasesendBeacon can't set custom headers, so it can't send X-Juju-Key. The key also has to be accepted in the URL (?juju_key=pk_…). That's safe because the public key is designed to be visible, which is one more reason the public/secret key split was worth it.
Breadcrumbs

What happened before the crash

A stack trace tells you where the code broke. Breadcrumbs tell you how the user got there.

10:41:02navigation/products → /cart
10:41:05clickbutton#apply-coupon
10:41:05fetchPOST /api/coupon → 500
10:41:05consolewarn "coupon response missing price"
10:41:05ERRORTypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'price')

The trace alone says lineTotal crashed. The breadcrumbs show the coupon API returned a 500 just before, which is the real bug.

BreadcrumbHow it's capturedWhat it reveals
consolewrap console.log/warn/errorwarnings the app printed just before
fetch / XHRwrap fetch and XMLHttpRequestfailed or slow API calls, the most common root cause
clicksone click listener on documentwhat the user did
route changeswrap history.pushState, listen for popstatewhich page they were on (single-page apps don't reload)
Ring bufferKeep the last 100. When a new one arrives, the oldest falls off. That matches the server's limit, and memory never grows however long the page stays open.
PrivacyFetch breadcrumbs record the method, URL and status code, never request or response bodies. Clicks record the element, not what the user typed. Bodies and inputs can hold passwords and personal data.
Public API

What developers type

import * as juju from "@juju/web";

juju.init({
  dsn: "https://pk_ceab7e46cedbf5149a110d37a668bfce@juju.example.com/1",
  release: "web@2.3.1",
  environment: "production",
});

try { riskyThing(); } catch (err) { juju.captureException(err); }  // handled errors too
juju.setUser({ id: "u_123" });                                      // after login

The prefilled value is an example. A DSN holds only the public key, so it's safe to ship inside an app.

  • dsn (Data Source Name) packs the server address, project id and public key into one copy-pasteable string. Developers set one value instead of three, so there's less to get wrong.
  • release makes errors actionable: "this started in 2.3.1" points at a deploy. Symbolication (Phase 5) needs it to pick the right source map, and the dashboard (Phase 6) needs it to detect regressions.
  • environment keeps staging noise out of production issues. The server defaults it to production, so staging must set it.
  • captureException reports errors the app caught but still wants to know about. The global hooks only see uncaught ones.
  • setUser turns "500 events" into "500 events affecting 3 users" or "affecting 480 users". That's how teams decide what to fix first.
Why keep it smallEvery published function is a promise you can't break later without breaking people's apps. It's the same lesson as versioning the event envelope.
Order

Why web comes before mobile

  1. Fastest feedback loop. Save, refresh, click "throw", see the issue. No simulators, no native builds.
  2. First real traffic for the server. Batching, gzip, partial acceptance and 429s get exercised by real client code instead of curl.
  3. @juju/core gets built and tested here, then React Native reuses it in Phase 3.
Done when

An error thrown while offline arrives exactly once after the browser reconnects.

That one test exercises the queue, retry, backoff, event_id and server-side dedupe together.
